what_it_does: This paper describes a specialized chip macro (a building block for larger chips) that performs matrix multiplication inside memory (called compute-in-memory or CIM) at extremely high efficiency: 51.6 trillion floating-point operations per watt. The innovation targets compound AI—a strategy where instead of running one massive language model, you run several smaller specialized models and combine their results. Prior CIM designs assumed Gaussian (normal distribution) data, which fails with the diverse data distributions that compound AI models produce. This paper's macro adapts to arbitrary data distributions, integrates efficient accumulation of partial mathematical results directly in memory (rather than shuttling data back and forth), and flexibly detects sparsity patterns that vary across different models. The design approaches the theoretical maximum speedup from sparsity (skipping unimportant numbers).
